blocks.title: ACT English — Practice Test 6
blocks.intro: Six essays, 50 questions, 35 minutes — the same length and timing as the English section of the enhanced ACT. In the real test, only 40 of the 50 questions are scored: the others are unscored field-test questions, and you cannot tell which ones they are. In this practice test, all 50 questions count. Answer every question: there is no penalty for wrong answers. After you finish, every answer choice has a short reason saying why it is right or wrong.

questions.p:
**Passage I: The Night Train to Aswan**

The summer I turned fifteen, my father announced that we would travel from Cairo to Aswan by train instead of by plane. I __[1] complained__ for a week. A flight would take little more than an hour, the train would take the whole night. "That is the point," my father said, and he refused to discuss it any further.

We boarded at Ramses Station just after seven in the evening. Our sleeping compartment was smaller then my bedroom at home, with two narrow beds that folded down from the wall and a tiny sink in the corner. A man in a white jacket brought us dinner on metal trays: rice, grilled chicken, and a small dish of rice pudding. I ate everything and, to my surprise, enjoyed it.

After dinner, I expected to fall asleep quickly. Instead, I sat at the window for hours while the train followed the Nile south. Villages slid past: a mosque's green light, a group of boys playing football under a single streetlamp, a donkey cart waiting at a crossing. My father, who had travelled on this line many times as a young engineer, named each town as we passed it.

Around midnight, the train stopped at a small station whose name I could not read in the dark. A woman climbed aboard with a basket of warm bread and offered it to everyone in our carriage. My father bought two loaves and gives one to the conductor, who thanked him and was grateful to him with a deep nod. Nevertheless, I understood something I had not understood in Cairo: the journey was not just the time between two places; it was a place of its own.

We reached Aswan at dawn. The river there seemed wider and bluer than in Cairo, and white-sailed feluccas were already moving between the dark granite islands. My father asked whether I still wished we had flown. The air was already warm, and a boatman was calling to us from the riverbank. I did not answer my father, but I have taken the night train every summer since.
questions.q: Question 1. Which choice is best for the underlined portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if the original is best.)
questions.e: "Complained" is precise and fits the relaxed but careful tone of the narrative. The strongest wrong choice, "registered my formal disapproval," is grammatical but sounds like an official letter, not a fifteen-year-old's reaction.
ce: Correct: "complained" is clear and matches the plain, personal tone of the story.
Far too formal and stiff for a teenager's story about a family trip.
Slang that does not fit the tone of the rest of the essay.
Says the same thing three times; one verb is enough.

questions.p:
**Passage II: Building with Earth**

In the 1940s, the Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy faced a problem that still troubles builders today. He had been asked to design a new village, New Gourna, on the west bank of the Nile near Luxor. The families who would live there had very little money, and concrete and steel __[11] was__ expensive. Fathy's solution was surprisingly simple, he would build with the earth beneath his feet. His answer would change the way many architects thought about building.

Mud brick had been used along the Nile for thousands of years, but by Fathy's time many Egyptians saw it as a material only for the poor. Fathy disagreed. Bricks made from local soil cost almost nothing, and thick mud walls keep rooms cool during the hot day and release warmth slowly at night. The real difficulty, which was the hardest problem of all, was the roof. Wood was scarce in Upper Egypt, so builders could not easily make the wooden frames normally needed to hold up a curved roof while its mortar set.

For example, Fathy found the answer in Nubia, far to the south. There, he met builders who still used an ancient method. They leaned each row of bricks against an end wall at a slight angle, so that every new row rested on the one before it. In this way, they could raise a vault or a dome with no wooden support at all. Fathy brought several Nubian masons to Gourna, and together they built houses, a mosque, a school, and they built a market.

Not everything went as planned. Many families did not want to leave their old homes, and the village was never completed as Fathy had imagined. Despite this, his ideas travelled much further than Luxor. In his book Architecture for the Poor, he argued that ordinary people could build beautiful, comfortable homes from local materials and traditional skills. Today, architects who design low-cost, climate-friendly buildings still look at his work a lot, and some of the mud-brick houses of New Gourna are still standing.

ce: The subject "concrete and steel" is two things joined by "and", so it needs a plural verb.
Singular and in the wrong tense for a story set in the 1940s.
Correct: plural to match "concrete and steel" and past tense to match "had".
Singular, and the present perfect does not fit the past setting.

**Passage III: Why Mars Is Red**

Even without a telescope, Mars is easy to spot in the night sky because of its reddish colour. For centuries, people __[21] wonders__ why the planet looks this way. Today, scientists know the answer: much of the surface of Mars is covered in rust. The ancient Romans, who saw the planet only as a red point of light, named it after their god of war.

The rocks and dust on Mars contain a great deal of iron. Over a very long time, this iron combined with oxygen, forming iron oxide; the same reddish material that appears on an old bicycle left out in the rain. Strong winds lift this fine dust into the thin air, and sometimes dust storms spread it across almost the entire planet.

For instance, the red dust also changes the colour of the sky. During the day, the Martian sky often looks pale orange or butterscotch. At sunset, however, the area around the Sun can glow blue, which is the opposite and reverse of the way that sunsets look here on our own planet, Earth. Wherever you look on Mars, the red dust leaves its mark.

questions.p:
**Passage IV: Every School Needs a Garden**

Most students learn that plants need sunlight, water, and soil. Far fewer have ever grown a single tomato. I believe that every school, even one in the middle of a crowded city, should have a garden that students plant and care for __[26] themself__.

The first reason is that a garden turns science into something students can touch. In a garden, lessons about seeds, roots, and insects stop being diagrams in a textbook. Students measure how fast bean plants grow, test which corner of the plot gets the most sun, and they keep records of the rainfall. Even a simple question, such as why one plant grew taller than its neighbour, becomes a real experiment. At one primary school in Giza, teachers noticed that pupils who worked in the school garden remembered their science lessons better than pupils who did not.

Second, a garden teaches patience and responsibility. A seed planted in October may not produce food until January, and if no one waters it, it will not produce anything at all. Students quickly get the picture that a garden depend on them. A class that forgets its watering rota for a week will see the results, and it is not a thing that needs a teacher to point them out to it.

Some people argue that school gardens cost too much money and take up valuable space. These concerns are understandable, but they are easy to answer. **Passage V: The Oud**

Few instruments are as closely linked to Arabic music as the oud. It has a rounded, pear-shaped body, a short neck, and strings that are usually arranged in pairs. Players pluck the strings with a long, thin plectrum called a __[36] risha, a word__ that means "feather" in Arabic.

Unlike a guitar, the oud has no frets, the thin metal bars that mark the notes along a guitars neck. Without frets, a player can slide smoothly from one note to the next and play the very small steps between notes that many Arabic melodies require. Many famous guitarists today play electric guitars with steel strings.

The oud also has a surprising connection to Europe. During the Middle Ages, the instrument travelled through Muslim Spain into other parts of Europe, where it developed into the lute. Even the name made the journey: the English word "lute" comes from the Arabic "al-ud," which means "the wood." Today, the oud is played in concert halls from Cairo to Paris, and its warm, deep sound is still at the heart of Arabic music.

**Passage VI: Up the Palm**

My uncle Saleh has grown dates in __[41] Siwa Oasis, deep in Egypt's Western Desert for__ most of his life. Last October, during the harvest, I spent two weeks working in his grove. I had imagined quiet afternoons in the shade. On my first morning, however, my uncle handed me a woven basket, pointed at a palm taller than our building in Cairo, and said, "Up you go."

Climbing a date palm is harder than it looks. My uncle showed me how to loop a strong rope around both my waist and the trunk and then I had to lean back against it while moving my feet up the rough bark. On the first day, I climbed about two metres before my legs began to shake. My uncle laughed, but not unkindly. "The palm is patient," he said. "You should be too." Each evening, my hands were sore and my knees were scraped, but I went back up every morning.

By the end of the first week, which was seven days later, I could reach the top.
